origin.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

definition_short: A piece with no safe square is attacked and lost, even though it is not currently pinned or forked.
definition_long:
Material is won not by a geometric double attack but by taking away every retreat first. Common victims: a queen that has grabbed a pawn deep in enemy territory, a bishop that has run out of diagonal after ...h6 and ...g5, and a knight on the rim.

ECM lists 'Trapping a piece' as a category. It is worth distinguishing from a fork because the winning move often attacks only ONE piece — the tactic is in the absence of squares, not in the presence of a second target.
epistemic_note: Motif (D). Detection needs mobility counting rather than line geometry, so it is a different kind of detector from the pin/skewer family.

preconditions: An enemy piece has no safe square available
It can be attacked by a unit it cannot capture or evade
indicators_for: The piece is deep in enemy territory or on the rim
Its own pawns block its retreat
indicators_against: It has a desperado capture that recovers the material
Trapping it costs more material than it is worth

exceptions: A trapped piece may escape by a desperado capture, or by a counter-threat that gains the tempo it needs.

explanation_templates.beginner: That piece has nowhere safe to go, so attacking it wins it.
explanation_templates.intermediate: The {piece} is trapped — every retreat square is covered.
explanation_templates.advanced: Trapped piece. Check for desperado resources and counter-threats before committing material to the hunt.
